chunks: Specifying a stepper motor. The question: How do you spec a stepper motor?
Specifying a stepper means choosing a motor that can actually do your job. You start from what the load needs: how much twist (torque), how fast, and how precisely.
Then you check that a candidate motor can deliver that twist at that speed.
Do not trust the big holding-torque number on the datasheet, because a stepper's torque drops as it spins faster.
Think of a person pushing a heavy cart. Standing still, they can push very hard. Once the cart must move fast, they run out of breath and push much less.
Holding torque is the standing-still push. The speed curve is the running push, and that is the one that matters.
The analogy breaks in one place: a stepper that runs out of push silently loses steps instead of slowing down.
The spec flow. The loop back to motor selection is normal: an inertia or thermal check often forces a different winding, frame or supply voltage.
Torque: the twisting effort a motor delivers, in newton-meters (N·m). Holding torque: torque at standstill. It is the zero-speed number only.
Pull-out torque: the most torque the motor gives at a given speed without skipping steps.
Torque-speed curve: the datasheet graph of pull-out torque at each speed, for a given supply voltage. Lead screw: a threaded rod that turns rotation into straight-line motion.
Its lead is the distance moved per turn.
A motor lifts a 2 kg carriage on an 8 mm lead screw that is about 35% efficient. Lifting it takes about 20 N. The screw turns that into about 0.
075 N·m of motor torque, once you allow for its losses. Double it for margin: 0. 15 N·m. Moving at 50 mm/s is 6.
25 screw turns per second, so a 200-step motor runs at 1250 full steps per second. Now read the torque-speed curve at your supply voltage, at 1250 steps per second.
If it shows at least 0. 15 N·m, the motor passes. That is the whole idea.
"I work backwards from the load: compute the torque including friction, gravity and acceleration, for example T equals FL over (2 pi ) for a lead screw, and the step rate needed for the speed.
Then I pick a motor whose pull-out torque at that speed and my supply voltage is at least 1. 5 to 2 times the requirement, not just a big holding torque.
I check inertia ratio, winding inductance versus speed, rated current and heating at hold, resolution with microsteps, frame size and shaft loads, and whether I need a closed-loop version."
